sources.headline: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
sources.text: Image source, Archaeological Legacy InstituteImage caption, A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object, which some had hypothesised could have been Amelia Earhart's plane, in a lagoon on NikumaroroByJacob PhillipsResearchers inspecting an object that some thought could have been the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote Pacific island say it is likely to be washed up trees.The team travelled to a lagoon in the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro, Kiribati, to confirm whether a shiny object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the decades-long mystery of the pioneering pilot's disappearance.But Purdue University, which has a leading role in the study, said the so-called Taraia Object "was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit".By the time the team arrived at the site a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment, the university said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937Images of the Taraia Object - which Purdue University said was visible in photography dating back to 1938 - led researchers to wonder if it was the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters."This mystery has been ongoing for 90 years and the mystery continues," said project director Rick Pettigrew, speaking from near the site of the object."The island has been holding on to its secrets and it continues to do so. I think eventually someone will find conclusive evidence here," he added.Earhart's plane vanished without a trace in 1937 on the third-to-last leg of her attempt to fly around the world.She had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea.Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to then travel towards Hawaii before returning to California.But their plane vanished while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote uninhabited coral island about 400 miles (644km) from Nikumaroro, to refuel.One theory is Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.The research team had travelled for five days by sea to reach Nikumaroro and was forced to spend several days on their ship following rough seas and strong winds, delaying their search on the island.They spent four days onshore investigating the site.

sources.headline: Amelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of trees
sources.text: A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solving the mystery of what happened to pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart has said an object they suspected to be her plane was a clump of washed-up trees.“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University, standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on the atoll of Nikumaroro, about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished in 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, leading to one of the largest air and sea searches in history. Nearly 90 years later, people are still looking, with Nikumaroro in the archipelago country of Kiribati emerging as a leading candidate for where they might have crash-landed.Previous visits to the uninhabited atoll have found signs of a castaway camp, a 1930s-era woman’s shoe and other tantalising evidence attributed to the celebrity aviator, including glass from a cosmetics freckle cream jar.The latest mission stemmed from 2020 satellite images showing an elongated, white object lying in the shallows of the island, near a sandy outcrop called the Taraia Peninsula.Other longtime Earhart explorers quickly identified it as a fallen tree, but Richard Pettigrew, who heads the nonprofit Archaeological Legacy Institute, found other images, including aerial video showing what he suspected to be a metallic glint in the water.After a multi-day voyage by ship and subsequent delays due to bad weather, the 17-person expedition managed to pass through the coral-encircled atoll and set up tents to conduct four days of research, including metal detecting. The crew was forced to sleep offshore, partly due to massive land-dwelling coconut crabs, known as “robber crabs” for their inquisitiveness when searching for food.Map showing location of Nikumaroro IslandBy Monday, Purdue University confirmed in a statement that the “visual anomaly” was “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit”.It said the glint was part of a natural process. “The fragment’s reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer. Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand.”The trip was partially sponsored by the university in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and mentored young female pilots, and which helped fund her modified Lockheed Electra 10-E, known as her “flying laboratory”.“While we know this is disappointing to many, including us, this mission adds a new chapter in the quest to find the ultimate answer to the mystery of what happened to Earhart during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe nearly nine decades ago,” the university statement said.The trip adds to a growing list of dismissed hypotheses, including that Earhart – who was the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight – was captured by Japanese forces or that she survived and lived under an alias.

sources.headline: What to Know About the Search for Amelia Earhart’s Plane
sources.text: A satellite image sent researchers to a remote Pacific atoll, but their findings brought no resolution to the decades-old search. Here’s what to know.

sources.headline: Object thought to be Amelia Earhart’s missing plane likely just 'large trees', researchers find
sources.text: An expedition to investigate if an anomaly seen on a satellite image of a remote island in the South Pacific was Amelia Earhart’s missing plane has ended without recovering the wreckage.

sources.headline: Expedition to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane comes up empty
sources.text:
By
Amanda Arden,
Jordan Freiman
News Editor

A mysterious object discovered near a remote Pacific island is not the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's missing plane, researchers said after an expedition to the site, dealing another setback to efforts to solve one of aviation's greatest mysteries nearly 90 years after the pilot disappeared."Evidence gathered at the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro confirmed that the visual anomaly first seen in satellite imagery in 2020 was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit," the researchers said. "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment," which they said is what they had initially hoped was the plane.The researchers said the reflective surface of the anomaly, which had led them to believe it could be metal, was the result of a carbonate veneer, noting other items found nearby were "similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand."On Oct. 14, a 17-member expedition team led by Purdue University's Steve Schultz and the Archaeological Legacy Institute's Richard Pettigrew launched an expedition to investigate a mysterious object that in aerial photos appeared to resemble possible wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane.Severe weather kept the research team aboard their ship for three of the five days allotted for the search, while limited fuel and supplies prevented them from extending the expedition. The search area was so remote, it took the team five days at sea to reach it.The expedition focused on a lagoon off Nikumaroro, where researchers examined the Taraia Object, an anomaly spotted by a Navy veteran in satellite imagery during the COVID pandemic. Although visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938, the object went unnoticed until 2020. Pettigrew said before reaching it that they believed it could be metal rather than a tree, but further investigation was needed to confirm its identity.
A satellite image shows the Taraia Object in a lagoon on Nikumaroro Island.
Rick Pettigrew, Archaeological Legacy Institute
"Amelia Earhart's spirit of courage and curiosity drove every step of the search," Pettigrew said Sunday. "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we're deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible. Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished."
The team had developed plans to photograph and film the lagoon and Taraia Object before using magnetometers and sonar equipment to survey the area. Researchers then planned to retrieve the object for identification. The Archaeology Channel documented the expedition through short video updates on its Heritage Broadcasting Service streaming platform.The research team previously said in a news release that there was "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared on July 2, 1937, roughly 22,000 miles into their trip. Earhart was attempting to become the first female pilot to circle the world, and the first pilot to do so around the equator, Earth's widest point.
American aviator Amelia Earhart at a refueling stop in Khartoum, Sudan, with the Lockheed Electra 10E in which she was attempting to circumnavigate the world with navigator Fred Noonan, on June 13, 1937.
Getty Images
Recently, President Trump ordered the declassification of records related to Earhart.
Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island lies about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were headed when they disappeared during their attempted flight around the world.Pettigrew believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro and survived there for some time. He points to relics dating to the 1930s and to human remains discovered on the island, which were later lost as possible evidence. However, several competing theories about the aviator's disappearance have emerged over the decades, many of which lack conclusive evidence.Researchers have spent decades searching for Earhart's plane, hoping its discovery could shed light on her disappearance. In 2024, an expedition team captured a sonar image of what appeared to be an aircraft on the ocean floor, but the object was later identified as a rock formation.
